column1: # id|status|note|sources (status: ok=confirmed, fix=corrected, disp=scholars disagree; noted, self=tradition's own account used)

mpb|fix|Qafzeh burials dated c. 92,000 years ago (thermoluminescence) with ochre and ochre-painted shells; wording adjusted to 'roughly 90,000–120,000 years ago'.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qafzeh_Cave;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_religion
gob|fix|Earliest dates c. 9500 calBC; start changed from 9600 to 9500 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion

pie|fix|Sky Father (*Dyḗws Ph₂tḗr), thunder god (*Perkʷunos), dawn goddess (*H₂éwsōs) and order (*h₂értus → ṛta, arəta) confirmed; archaic PIE dated c. 4500–4000 BCE so start moved to 4500 BCE; horse-sacrifice and guest–host claims removed from the description as not confirmed in the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Indo-European_mythology

upa|ok|Lion-man figurine c. 38,000 BCE; shamanism inferred for the Upper Paleolithic; meaning of 'Venus' figurines debated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_religion

neo|ok|Çatalhöyük c. 7500–5700 BCE; Neolithic burials inside houses and plastered skulls in the Levant.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_religion
meg|ok|Newgrange 3200–3100 BCE; Stonehenge initial form 3100 BCE, final c. 2600 BCE, use ended c. 1600 BCE; solstice alignment.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion

zor|disp|Britannica: Zarathustra 'flourished before the 6th century BCE'; dates remain disputed (estimates c. 1500–500 BCE). Bridge of the Requiter (Chinvat), heaven/hell, resurrection, savior (Saoshyant), fire cult and influence on Judaism, Christianity and Islam all confirmed.|https://www.britannica.com/topic/Zoroastrianism

par|fix|Britannica dates Parsi emigration to India 'from the 10th century onward'; start moved from 800 to 900 CE and the description notes the traditional earlier date (Qissa-i Sanjan).|https://www.britannica.com/topic/Zoroastrianism
zur|fix|Britannica: Zurvan (Time) as father of Ohrmazd and Ahriman; wording changed from 'above both' to 'father of both'.|https://www.britannica.com/topic/Zoroastrianism

sum|ok|Gods tended in temples by priests; humans created to serve the gods; dim underworld (Irkalla); Gilgamesh holds the earliest flood reference.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Mesopotamian_religion

akk|fix|Mesopotamian religion 'had almost completely died out by approximately 400–500 AD', with temples revived in Assyrian vassal states in the Parthian period; end moved from 300 to 400 CE. Marduk made supreme under Hammurabi (18th c. BCE); description reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Mesopotamian_religion

har|disp|Harranian polytheism with planetary cults survived into the Islamic era; in 830 al-Ma'mun's ultimatum led them to adopt the name Sabians. Hermetic/Neoplatonic identity attested by medieval sources but with 'no firm evidence'; end date uncertain (11th c.). Description softened.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabians

egy|fix|Pharaoh identified with Horus, Ma'at, ka/ba confirmed; Philae closure dated AD 537 (Procopius), though Dijkstra argues organized cult ended in the 5th c.; end moved from 550 to 537.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion

ate|ok|Akhenaten replaced Amun with the Aten; monotheism vs. monolatry/henotheism is disputed; reign began 1353 or 1351 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion
kem|ok|Egyptian revival movements date to the 1970s.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion
kus|ok|Nubians adopted Amun worship. Apedemak not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egyptian_religion
kan|ok|El heads the pantheon with Asherah; Baal (Hadad) storm god, Anat, Mot; Ugaritic texts c. 1275 BCE, Ugarit destroyed c. 1200 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Canaanite_religion
pho|disp|Melqart, Tanit and Baal Hammon confirmed; child sacrifice at Carthage remains debated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Canaanite_religion
isr|disp|Whether Asherah was worshipped as Yahweh's consort is debated (some read ʾašērāh as 'holy place'); description now says 'possibly'.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Canaanite_religion

ara|ok|Hubal, al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt; sacred stones; Kaaba as pre-Islamic pilgrimage site; jinn; Jewish, Christian and ḥanīf communities.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia

nab|fix|Dushara was the Nabataean patron god; god-stones were often carved in rock faces and could bear incised features, so 'plain aniconic stones' was overstated. Reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia

myc|fix|Date range c. 1600–1100 BCE confirmed. Linear B names Poseidon (po-se-da-o) and Dionysus (di-wo-nu-so); Hera only via an epithet in the checked source, so the description no longer lists Zeus and Hera as named.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_religion
grk|ok|No revealed scripture; Delphi oracle; official persecution under Theodosius I from 381 culminating in the 391–392 decrees.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_religion

orp|part|Soul held in bondage by the Titanic body and reincarnated until initiation, poems attributed to Orpheus, 6th–5th c. BCE origins confirmed. Orphic vegetarianism is not covered by the checked source (it is attested in Plato, Laws 782c).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orphism_(religion)
pyt|ok|Pythagoras taught reincarnation.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_religion

ele|fix|Earliest textual source is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (c. 650 BCE), so start moved from 600 to 650 BCE; afterlife reward confirmed; men, women and slaves initiated after c. 300 BCE (Greek speakers without blood guilt); closed by Theodosius I in 392, shrines looted by Alaric in 396.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleusinian_Mysteries
cyb|fix|Phrygian 'Matar Kubileya' inscription dates to the 6th c. BCE, so start moved from 800 to 600 BCE; arrival in Rome 204 BCE and eunuch galli confirmed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cybele

hel|fix|Organized revival in Greece from the 1990s and recognized as a 'known religion' in 2017 confirmed; adherents are divided on animal sacrifice, and the description now says so.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenism_(modern_religion)

mit|disp|Popular in the Roman army from the 1st to 4th c. CE; origins disputed (1st c. BCE or CE); largely men only; seven grades; sacred banquets; underground mithraea; Iranian link debated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mithraism

cel|part|Roman reports of human sacrifice (possibly exaggerated) plus rare archaeological evidence; gradual conversion from the 5th c. Medieval Irish sources record Beltaine, Lughnasadh, Samhain and Imbolc, but it is unclear which festivals the ancient Celts held, so the description is softened. Caesar's report of transmigration is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Celtic_religion
dru|ok|Ancient Order of Druids founded 1781; Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids founded 1964 by Ross Nichols.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_paganism

nor|fix|Iceland adopted Christianity at the Althing in 999 (often given as 1000); Sweden fully Christian by the early 12th c.; Yggdrasil, Valhalla, Ragnarök and seiðr confirmed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Norse_religion
sla|ok|Perun and Veles; Svetovid's temple at Arkona destroyed in 1168 by Valdemar I; Christianization between the 8th and 13th c.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavic_paganism
rod|fix|The checked source dates the organized revival to the early 20th century, so start moved from 1980 to 1930.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavic_paganism

bal|part|Dievas the sky god and Saule confirmed; the checked source places Baltic Christianization from the 15th c. Lithuania's 1387 baptism is the standard date but was not covered by this source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_religion

wic|fix|Wheel of the Year (eight festivals) and Goddess/God duotheism confirmed; Gardner claimed initiation in 1939 and publicized Wicca in 1954.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_paganism;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion

mar|fix|Mari native religion has existed continuously alongside Orthodoxy, with about 15% of Mari El's population identifying with it (2004 survey). The 'Europe's last pagan religion' tagline was removed because the checked source does not use it.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_paganism

man|fix|Mani born 216 near Ctesiphon; saw himself as completing Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus; the Elect abstained from meat and wine. In China it was banned by the Ming in 1370 and absorbed into Buddhism and Daoism by the end of the 14th c., with a remnant at the Cao'an temple. End moved from 1600 to 1400.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manichaeism;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_religion
yaz|ok|Sheikh Adi died 1162; seven angels led by Tawûsî Melek; rebirth ('changing of the shirt'); Lalish pilgrimage; strict endogamy.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yazidism

yar|fix|Sultan Sahak dated to the late 14th c., so start moved from 1350 to 1380; successive divine manifestations and transmigration; Kalâm-e Saranjâm from the 15th c.; c. 0.5–1 million in Iran plus 75,000–250,000 in Iraq.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yarsanism

maz|fix|Prominent under Kavad I (r. 498–531); communal ownership, opposed war and meat-eating. Killed by Khusrau I; the 'massacre in 528' detail was replaced with 'executed under Khusrau I'.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazdakism
tng|fix|Tengri first appears in Chinese chronicles in the 4th c. BCE as the Xiongnu sky god, so start moved from 300 to 350 BCE; Umay; revival since the 1990s.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tengrism
bur|ok|Altaian Burkhanism (1904).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tengrism

kar|fix|The checked source dates Karaism to the early 9th c., with Anan ben David's 8th-c. movement as forerunner; start moved from 760 to 800.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements

ref|disp|The checked source says Reform began c. 1820. Israel Jacobson's Seesen temple (1810) is the conventional first milestone, so 1810 is kept and noted as an early milestone.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements

ort|fix|Orthodoxy became a self-conscious movement in opposition to Reform; the first separate Orthodox congregation (S. R. Hirsch, Frankfurt) dates to 1851. Start moved from 1820 to 1840, at low confidence.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements

con|part|The checked source says Conservative Judaism originated in 19th-c. Germany and was institutionalized in the US. The JTS founding date (1886) was not covered.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements
rec|ok|A 1922 American split from Conservative Judaism led by Mordecai Kaplan.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements
hjd|ok|Founded in Detroit in 1963 by Rabbi Sherwin Wine; Society for Humanistic Judaism founded 1969.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements
has|ok|Founded by Israel ben Eliezer, the Baal Shem Tov (1700–1760); 1740 is an approximate start.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements
sad|fix|Lost prominence with the Temple's fall in 70 CE but probably continued informally for decades; end moved from 70 to 100.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_religious_movements

smr|disp|About 900 people (2024); Passover lamb sacrifice on Mount Gerizim continues; Samaritan Pentateuch only. The schism date is widely debated (a gradual process, with a decisive break often placed in the Hasmonean period), so start moved from 400 to 300 BCE at low confidence.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samaritans

sab|fix|Sabbatai Zevi proclaimed himself messiah in 1665 and converted to Islam on 15 September 1666; Dönmeh descendants persisted into 21st-c. Turkey. End changed to 1950 (as an organized religion), with a note.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbateans
fra|ok|Jacob Frank's 18th-c. Sabbatean movement in Eastern Europe; Frank converted to Catholicism.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbateans

bet|disp|Scholars disagree. One school (Kaplan, Shelemay, Tamrat) sees the community forming in the 14th–16th c.; another (Messing, Waldman) sees ancient Jewish roots; the community's own account traces descent to the tribe of Dan. Start moved from 600 to 1350 at low confidence, with both views in the description. About 173,500 worldwide, mostly in Israel after Operations Moses (1984) and Solomon (1991).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Israel

kab|ok|Sefer ha-Bahir from 12th–13th-c. Provence; Zohar late 13th c. (Moses de León); sefirot and Ein Sof; Luria in 16th-c. Safed; shattering of the vessels, tikkun, gilgul.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabbalah
lur|ok|Luria systematized shevirat ha-kelim, tikkun and gilgul in 16th-c. Safed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabbalah

arm|disp|Tiridates III made Christianity the state religion 'between 300 and 301' by tradition; estimates range from 284 to 314 (Garsoïan favors 314). About 9 million adherents (church figure). The matagh offering is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Apostolic_Church

eth|fix|Aksum Christianized c. 330, autocephaly 1959, about 60 million adherents worldwide; Saturday kept alongside Sunday; a tabot in every church; unclean meats avoided; about 250 fast days a year. Circumcision is a cultural custom, not a religious requirement (the liturgy rejects circumcision 'like the Jews'), so that trait was removed and the description fixed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church

shk|fix|Founded c. 1747 by the Wardleys after breaking from the Quakers; Ann Lee recognized in 1770 as Christ's second appearing; celibacy; ecstatic, later choreographed, dance. Three members as of 2025 after one joined Sabbathday Lake in August 2025; description updated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakers

mon|disp|Founded by Montanus with Prisca and Maximilla. The start date is debated (c. 135–177 CE); the movement persisted locally into the 6th c. (Justinian's measures 530–550; Tascodrugites c. 600).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montanism

coe|fix|Declared independence in 424 under Catholicos Dadishoʿ, and already a separate organization by 431, so start moved from 431 to 424. Reached China in 635 (Alopen); Xi'an Stele 781; successors are the Assyrian and Ancient Churches of the East. Aniconism became the norm but was not absolute.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_East
jin|ok|Alopen reached Chang'an in 635; the Xi'an Stele was erected on 7 January 781.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_East

kim|ok|Kimbangu's healing ministry began in April 1921; jailed by Belgian authorities until his death in 1951; alcohol, tobacco, polygamy and dancing prohibited; the church holds Kimbangu to be the Holy Spirit (controversial); Baptist roots; c. 6 million by church estimate.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimbanguist_Church

zcc|fix|Founded in 1910 by Engenas Lekganyane (not 1924); 4.97 million members in the 2001 census; healing, no alcohol or tobacco, Easter pilgrimage to Moria. Called 'one of the largest' (not 'the largest') African-initiated churches. Pork and ancestor claims not confirmed, so those traits were removed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zion_Christian_Church

alad|part|Developed in SW Nigeria from c. 1918 amid health crises; Cherubim and Seraphim (1925), Church of the Lord (1930), Christ Apostolic Church revival (1930); prayer, faith healing and visions. White garments not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladura

duk|fix|First recorded in 1701 (origins uncertain); rejected priests and icons; c. 7,000 burned weapons in 1895; c. 7,500 reached Canada in 1899; vegetarian by the late 1880s. 1,675 self-identified in Canada's 2021 census. Start moved from 1700 to 1701.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doukhobors
hut|ok|Communes formed in 1528 in Tyrol; near-total community of goods; 58,392 people in 544 colonies (2024).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutterites
nic|ok|Council of Nicaea 325; Edict of Thessalonica 380.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
roc|ok|East–West schism 1054; Second Lateran Council mandated clerical celibacy in 1139.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
eor|ok|East–West schism 1054.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
oor|ok|Council of Chalcedon 451.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
don|ok|Donatist schism 311–314 (the checked timeline gives 314 for the formal condemnation).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
wal|ok|Waldensians founded 1173; declared heretical 1215.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
lol|ok|Wycliffe's Bible 1380–82; Lollard Twenty-five Articles 1388.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
hus|ok|Jan Hus executed during the Council of Constance (1414–18).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
lut|ok|95 Theses 1517.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
cal|ok|Zwingli began reform preaching in Zurich in 1519 (council adopted it in 1523); Calvin's Geneva from 1536/1541.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
prs|ok|Scottish Reformation 1560.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
bap|ok|First Baptist church (John Smyth) 1609.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
ami|ok|Amish split 1693.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
met|ok|Wesley's Aldersgate experience 1738; field preaching from 1739.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
eva|ok|First Great Awakening 1730–1749.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
lds|ok|Church of Christ founded 6 April 1830 (Book of Mormon published 1830).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
sda|ok|Seventh-day Adventist Church organized 1863.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
sal|ok|Salvation Army 1865.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
chs|ok|Christian Science church 1879.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
qua|disp|The checked timeline dates George Fox's movement to 1648; 1652 (Pendle Hill vision) is the conventional founding year; both noted.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
jw|ok|Zion's Watch Tower started 1879; the name Jehovah's Witnesses was adopted in 1931.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
men|ok|Menno Simons left Catholicism in 1536 (died 1561).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity
olb|ok|Nikon's reforms and the Raskol 1653–1666; Avvakum burned 1682.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity

okc|ok|The Old Catholic movement formed after Vatican I (1870), joining the Church of Utrecht, which had been independent since the early 18th c.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Christianity

drz|fix|Divine call opened 30 May 1017; new pledges ended 1043 and conversion closed by 1046; reincarnation only into human bodies; c. 0.8–1 million adherents (up to 2 million). Al-Hakim is awaited from occultation, but Druze texts warn against treating any human as God, so the 'divine incarnation' trait was removed and the description reworded. Druze do not identify as Muslims (Ismaili origin noted).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druze
ala|ok|Ibn Nusayr (d. c. 868); triad of Ali (Maʿna), Muhammad (Ism) and Salman (Bab); reincarnation; c. 2–3 million worldwide.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alawites

alv|disp|Roots in Seljuk-era (11th–12th c.) Turkmen Sufi, pro-Alid Islam; the start date of 1500 marks the Safavid-era crystallization of Kizilbash identity. Cem with semah performed by men and women together; worship in the cemevi; linked to Haji Bektash; c. 4–15% of Turkey (some estimates 20–25 million).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alevism

bek|fix|Evolved in 13th-c. Anatolia, rituals systematized by Balım Sultan (1509–16); official order of the Janissaries, banned 1826; headquarters in Tirana from 1930; ritual use of rakia ('dem'). A formal Allah–Muhammad–Ali triad is not described in the checked source, so that trait was removed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bektashi_Order

bah|ok|The Báb began teaching in 1844 and was executed in 1850; Baháʼu'lláh's 1863 claim; progressive revelation; elected assemblies and the Universal House of Justice with no clergy; alcohol forbidden; Nineteen-Day Fast; daily obligatory prayer; c. 7–8 million adherents.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith
bab|ok|The Báb began teaching in 1844 and was executed in 1850.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith

noi|fix|Founded July 1930 in Detroit by Wallace Fard Muhammad, who is taught to be God in person; Elijah Muhammad; Farrakhan rebuilt it in 1977; Malcolm X left in March 1964; pork, alcohol and tobacco forbidden. The Nation rejects any afterlife, so judgment/soul traits were removed and materialism added.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation_of_Islam
msta|part|Founded in 1913 in Newark by Noble Drew Ali; a key source for the Nation of Islam. The Circle Seven Koran is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nation_of_Islam

dil|disp|Founded 1582 at Fatehpur Sikri; defunct c. 1605; only 19 identified followers; sun and light veneration with a fire ritual; vegetarianism. Scholars debate whether it was a religion or a discipleship around Akbar. Fire trait added.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Din-i_Ilahi

wah|ok|1744 pact with Muhammad bin Saud; condemned saint veneration and shrine pilgrimage as shirk; often treated as a subset of Salafism. 'Wahhabi' is an exonym that followers reject, and the entry is renamed accordingly.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahhabism

suf|fix|Usually dated to early Islam, partly as an ascetic reaction under the Umayyads (Hasan al-Basri, d. 728), so start moved from 750 to 700; dhikr, silsila, Ibn Arabi's wahdat al-wujud; samāʿ.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufism
chi|ok|Moinuddin Chishti (1141–1236) settled at Ajmer; the Chishtiyya use samāʿ but prohibit dancing with intent.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufism

ebu|disp|Buddha's birth c. 563 or c. 480 BCE, death between 411 and 400 BCE in recent dating; the start date of 450 BCE is a midpoint at medium confidence.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism

sthv|ok|First schism into Sthavira and Mahāsāṃghika 'probably after the time of Ashoka', or at the Second Council (383 or c. 330 BCE).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
mhs|ok|Mahāsāṃghika and sub-groups (Lokottaravāda, Caitika and others).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
pud|ok|Sthavira offshoot founded by Vātsīputra, c. 3rd c. BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
sar|ok|Northwest India and Kashmir.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
the|ok|Mahinda brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka c. 250–220 BCE; Pali Canon written down in 29 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
mah|ok|Mahāyāna sutras date back to the 1st c. BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
mdh|ok|Nāgārjuna c. 150–250 CE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
yga|ok|Founded in the 4th c. CE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
cha|ok|Bodhidharma settles at Shaolin in 527 (traditional).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
tnd|ok|Saichō went to China in 804 and founded Tendai on his return (805).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
shg|ok|Kūkai went to China in 804 and founded Shingon on his return (806).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
jod|ok|Hōnen (1133–1212) founded Pure Land as an independent sect.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
zen|ok|Dōgen brought Sōtō from China in 1227.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
nch|ok|Nichiren born 1222; began preaching in 1253.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
gel|ok|First Dalai Lama Gendun Drubpa (1391–1474).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
kag|ok|Marpa introduced Sarma lineages in the 11th c.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
sgi|ok|Founded 1930.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
nav|ok|Ambedkar's mass conversion in 1956.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Buddhism
hoa|ok|Founded 1939 by Huỳnh Phú Sổ.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
wbu|ok|Korean reformed Buddhism (Wonbulgyo).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
vip|ok|20th-century lay meditation movement.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_of_Buddhism
lin|ok|Established by Basavanna in the 12th c.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
kas|ok|Vasugupta and lineage, including Abhinavagupta.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
smt|ok|Credited to Shankara, with mathas at Sringeri, Kanchi, Puri, Dwarka and Jyotir; five-deity pañcāyatana pūjā.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
swa|ok|Follows Sahajanand Swami (Swaminarayan).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
vis|ok|Śrī Vaiṣṇavism with Ramanuja as principal ācārya.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
dvt|ok|Brahma Sampradāya following Madhvācārya.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
gau|ok|Chaitanya Sampradāya following Chaitanya Mahāprabhu.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_denominations
